unit.can_do_en: plan a walk in the forest and talk about berries.

lines.speaker: Leena
lines.gloss_en: Shall we go to the forest on Sunday?

judge.reason: Both ask 'Shall we go to the forest on Sunday?'; only register differs.
Joo and Kyllä both mean 'yes'; the question is identical.

lines.speaker: Leena
lines.gloss_en: In Nuuksio. You can get there by bus.

judge.reason: Nuuksios/Nuuksiossa and bussil/bussilla are the same place and means of transport.

lines.speaker: Leena
lines.gloss_en: Good shoes, a packed lunch and a thermos.

judge.reason: termari is the colloquial form of termospullo (thermos); same list.
Both ask 'Are there bears there?'; only register differs.

lines.speaker: Leena
lines.text_puhe: Ei Nuuksios. Mut siel on kauniita järviä.
lines.text_kirja: Ei Nuuksiossa. Mutta siellä on kauniita järviä.
lines.gloss_en: Not in Nuuksio. But there are beautiful lakes.

judge.reason: Same negation, place and statement about beautiful lakes; mut/mutta and siel/siellä are register variants.

puhe.text: Ei Nuuksios. Mut siel on kauniita järviä.

kirja.text: Ei Nuuksiossa. Mutta siellä on kauniita järviä.

judge.reason: Both say 'Lovely. I'm coming!'; mä tuun and minä tulen are the same.

Minä with -n: minun pitää means I have to. Speech shortens it to mun.

forms.form_name_en: present tense, 3rd person singular, with the question ending -ko/-kö
forms.why_en: On with -ko to ask a question. Speech often says -ks: onks.
Siellä means there. Speech shortens -llä to -l: Siellä becomes Siel.
Asking if there are any takes -ja: karhu becomes karhuja.
Ei on its own answers 'no'. People say it the same way.
Speech shortens mutta to mut. Books write mutta.
Plural 'some' takes -ita: kaunis becomes kauniita.
Plural 'some' takes -iä: järvi becomes järviä.
The partitive singular is used in exclamations: ihana becomes ihanaa!
Speech shortens minä to mä. Books write minä.
Adds -en for 'I': tulla becomes tulen. Speech says tuun.
